title: Position: Sustainable Open-Source AI Requires Tracking the Cumulative Footprint of Derivatives
claim: Resource-intensive infrastructure concentrates where environmental stress is already high, and model footprints differ by orders of magnitude, so impact is hidden.
layout: 2 panels, left map then right bar chart, dual y-axes
description: Two panels side by side. Panel A is a choropleth map of the contiguous United States, with watershed regions shaded from blue (low water stress, about 1.0) to deep red (high, about 2.0 and above). White circles sit on top, sized by the number of data centres per state. The top ten states carry bold counts: 568, 392, 288, 197, 194, 195, 155, 133, 121 and 107. A horizontal diverging colorbar labelled Water Stress Level sits at the bottom left. Panel B is a grouped bar chart with two dual y-axes. Orange bars show CO2 emissions (tCO2eq) on the left axis, and blue bars show water consumption in megalitres on the right axis. It compares a Closed Model (estimated GPT-4: 11,000 tCO2eq and 150 ML) with an Open Model (Llama 3-8B: 2,290 tCO2eq and 22 ML). The eye goes first to the red-blue map and the large circles, then to the tall closed-model bars.
caption: The hidden environmental reality of the AI ecosystem. (A) Localized water stress across the United States, according to [ref]. Circles illustrate the number of data centres per state (\url{https://www.datacentermap.com/usa/}), with the top 10 states labelled with their respective counts. Texas (392), California (288), and Arizona (155) are among the states that have both a high number of data centres and high water stress levels. (B) Estimated order-of-magnitude comparison of training-related carbon and water footprints. Closed-model values (e.g., GPT-4) are approximate and based on secondary public estimates rather than audited disclosures [ref]. Open-model values (e.g., Llama 3) are drawn from official Meta documentation [ref] when available. Water consumption values for both model types are estimated using reported/inferred energy consumption and average water usage effectiveness (WUE) factors.
abstract: Open-source AI is scaling rapidly, and model hubs now host millions of artifacts. Each foundation model can spawn large numbers of fine-tunes, adapters, quantizations, merges, and forks. We take the position that compute efficiency alone is insufficient for sustainability in open-source AI. Lower per-run costs can accelerate experimentation and deployment, increasing aggregate footprint unless impacts are measurable and comparable across derivative lineages. However, the energy use, water consumption, and emissions of these derivative lineages are rarely measured or disclosed in a consistent, comparable way, leaving aggregate ecosystem impact largely invisible. We argue that sustainable open-source AI requires a coordination infrastructure that tracks impacts across model lineages, not only base models. We propose Data and Impact Accounting (DIA), a lightweight, non-restrictive transparency layer that (i) standardizes carbon-and-water reporting metadata, (ii) integrates low-friction measurement into common training and inference pipelines, and (iii) aggregates reports via public dashboards to summarize cumulative impacts across releases and derivatives. DIA makes derivative costs visible and supports ecosystem-level accountability while preserving openness. Project Page: https://vectorinstitute.github.io/ai-impact-accounting/
